en: Supplementary Records from the Zhīyuán Collection:
Record of the Turning Wheel Repository at Shùngǎn Monastery in Tāizhōu; Record of the Prabhūtaratna Stupa at Pùzhào Monastery in Xiùzhōu;
Record of the Amitābha Image at Wúliàng Monastery in Lín'ān; Record of the Repair of the Main Hall at Cídé Monastery in Tāizhōu.
Record of the Precious Pavilion of Amitābha at Longquan in Yuezhou; Record of the Three-Saint Standing Images at Jingyuan in Mingzhou;
Record of the Wheel Repository (Lunzang) at Shunganyuan in Taizhou;
[and] the crushing of mulberry bark to make paper, the smelting of soot to make ink, and the gathering of hair and cutting of bamboo to make brushes for the execution of strokes and characters.
The characters are formed by combining strokes; characters have invocations that serve as names; names are accumulated to form phrases; phrases are accumulated to form stanzas;

stanzas are accumulated to form fascicles; and fascicles are accumulated to form volumes. By means of this, the words of the Sages are recorded and handed down to posterity as a model that may be followed and not altered;
therefore, they are called "Jing" (Scriptures). I have often examined the reasons for their formation.
The sutras are all conditioned things within heaven and earth, produced by human effort;
they are composed of paper, silk, ink, brush, wood, earth, water, and fire. Their names, phrases, and verses are made of worldly characters, speech, and empty sounds.
Their creation is the gathering together of craftsmen’s skill, discernment, and vital energy.
All these arise from a multitude of conditions; yet each, in itself, has no name, and it is people who forcibly bestow names upon them.
When people who employ such forced names encounter objects to which they have assigned forced names, the sūtra is thereby formed—and thus the sūtra, too, is a forced name.
If this is so, where indeed does the Buddha’s sūtra truly reside? Nevertheless, when there is even a single moment of faithful acceptance, recitation, and upholding, [the sūtra is realized].
Among those who rejoice, there are indeed some who eliminate transgressions, some who escape suffering, some who generate merit, some who attain awakening, and some who realize personhood;
even up to the ocean of the Perfectly All-Knowing One adorned with the myriad practices, none arise except through this.
Thus, how could the Buddha’s sutras be found elsewhere than in paper, silk, brush, ink, words, phrases, and verses? It is through these that they are fashioned.

There is no craft that is not within the sutras, as was sought previously; yet, when one seeks to realize them, there is absolutely nothing that corresponds to their names, let alone anything possessing actual reality.
Observing it from this perspective, there is not a single thing that is not real, much less its name.
Thus, the sutras of our Buddha cannot be said to exist, nor can they be said to be non-existent; they cannot be sought within, without, or in between.

It cannot be expressed in words nor fathomed by intellectual deliberation; if one can penetrate this, then neither the "attainer" nor the "attained" is seen, and both subject and object vanish together, such that acceptance and rejection are both forgotten.
In that state, all is profoundly still and universally pure. Thus, though the hands do not hold a scroll, one is constantly reading this sutra;
though the mouth does not cease its recitation, not a single character has been moistened by ink. Therefore, with every phrase and every verse, it passes through the ears and over the eyes.
Although the merit of giving away one’s body and life as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is not considered much, how much less so for those who have attained profound realization?

Therefore, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, the Tathāgata sacrificed his head and eyes, abandoned his kingdoms and cities, humbled himself to serve as a bed and seat, and spread his hair as a mat.
He sought this through the company of the sages; he manifested birth and proclaimed nirvana within lands as numerous as motes of dust, illustrating the causes and conditions thereof.
These teachings were expounded according to the needs of the occasion; after the Parinirvāṇa, they were compiled by Kāśyapa and Ānanda.
They were preserved through twenty-four patriarchs and translated by An Shigao and Kumārajīva. Subsequently, Faxian and Xuanzang searched for and retrieved them.

Although the scriptures are immeasurable, based on those translated in the Eastern Land of China, there are more than five thousand fascicles. These have spread far and wide, awakening those who were deluded and obstructed.
Among them, those who have turned from the heterodox back to the orthodox and whose conscious minds have realized the fundamental source are beyond counting.

The Great Being of Dongyang, a holy one in his final birth before Buddhahood, desiring to universally plant the conditions for deliverance through the Dragon Flower, gathered the various sections of the scriptures—both great and small—and placed them in precious caskets.
These were arranged upon tiered pavilions, secured with mechanical devices, and adorned with gold and colors, being designated as the "Turning Wheel."
Thus, within the Sūtra-piṭaka, the great thousand-fold world-system scroll of the Vairocana Ocean-treasury remains quiescent and unmoving, yet its turning is inexhaustible.
Some merely see it turn and thereby give rise to faith; some, because of its turning, realize that it has never actually turned;
and some abide in non-turning while following its constant turning throughout the day. Whether of superior wisdom or inferior folly, each acts according to their own capacity.

Because it yielded great benefit, the Wheel Treasury (Lunzang) began at the Twin Śāla Trees; subsequently, other temples all followed this example, and it became especially prevalent in Eastern Zhejiang.
Although there is no documentary evidence for this, might it not be one aspect of a skillful means for guiding and attracting [devotees]?
At Shungan Temple in Taicheng, during the Tianfu era of the Shu Jin dynasty, the local official Hu Dushi donated his residence to establish it; it was originally named Baoguo. Now...

In the early years of the Shaoxiang era of the Northern Song dynasty, the temple was granted its current name. Successive generations of masters and disciples resided there in turn, yet for a long time they failed to find suitable successors;

consequently, the community fell into profound decline. In the tenth year of the Xining era, the local official Lin Hua and his younger brother, the monk Xi-zhan, joined forces to solicit donations and constructed a revolving sutra repository (*dharmacakra-piṭaka*), as well as a Dharma hall, a monks' hall, a triple-gate entrance, a bell and drum tower, dormitories, corridors, a kitchen, and a storehouse.
In these twenty years alone, the work of restoration and expansion has not ceased; the expenditure is estimated at no less than ten million coins.

From the wheel-store (dharani-casket) that was produced, funds were used to establish the Changtang Hall to receive the assembly from across the seas. Consequently, men and women vied with one another to offer fields and acres to provide for the two daily meals.
Every summer, they invite Dharma masters to lecture and preach for the sake of transformation and guidance, while incense, lamps, mirrors, and chanting resound morning and evening.
Without interrupting my duties, I have been entrusted with the command to compose a record for the altar established at Jingde [Monastery] within the Upper Hall of the *Lengyan* [Sutra].

Linhua Xizhan has repeatedly requested this memorial; I humbly reflect that those who call themselves Buddhists claim that the Way does not reside in language or written characters, yet there are those who neglect the scriptural teachings.
Or perhaps they rely on these very texts for recitation, seeking only fame and profit, or using them as mere ornamentation.
Among those who possess a single body, there are some who benefit from this [temple] yet do not fear sin or merit, and there are those who employ it unjustly;
how could one have expected that a layman serving as a public official would be able to venerate and establish [this site], exerting his utmost strength to provide external protection such as this?
Thus, are we not to feel ashamed? Therefore, I have recorded its beginning and end to inform my fellow practitioners.
Record of the Many Treasures Stūpa at Puzhao Monastery in Xiuzhou:
Upon Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the Unsurpassed Dharma King assembled hundreds of thousands of myriads of beings to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Suddenly, a precious stūpa surged forth from the earth, standing tall and majestic above the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings. Flower garlands rained down, and dragons and spirits attended upon it.
From within the stupa, a voice resounded, praising the words of truth spoken by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni;
the great assembly was struck with wonder and doubt, not knowing its origin. The World-Honored One declared: "This is the whole-body stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna from long ago.
He made this great vow: 'After my parinirvāṇa, if in the lands of the ten directions this sutra is preached, my stupa shall emerge to bear witness.'"
When the assembly heard this praise, they were filled with joy and all desired to pay their respects.

At that time, the World-Honored One, employing his great spiritual power, performed three transformations of the land, causing his emanations to gather from afar. He then raised his right finger and opened the door of the stupa;

the assembly beheld that Buddha, majestic and as if alive, who then offered half of his seat to Śākyamuni so that they might sit side by side. Thereupon, the World-Honored One, responding to this, charged Mahākāśyapa:

After earnestly entrusting the circulation [of this teaching] to the assembly, he finally dispersed the gathering, and the stupa likewise vanished. I humbly reflect that the Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause;
yet sentient beings were so attached to desire that their strength was insufficient to bear it. For over forty years, he kept it secret and did not transmit it.
Only when those of great capacity were ready to receive it did he suddenly manifest his perfect voice, thundering forth to point all transformations back to the single principle.
The three vehicles are united under one path; once the jewel from the topknot is released, the precious chariot is bestowed equally.

Thus, the manifestation of spiritual power is proclaimed, fulfilling long-held aspirations. As we prepare to return to the ultimate truth, there remains sorrow for those yet to be delivered; may this wondrous Way descend upon all eternity.
Since the Way is upheld by humans and the seeds of existence arise through conditions, the Buddhas of antiquity manifested extraordinary and sublime omens.
The Original Teacher also earnestly charged [his disciples], and caused the boundless Mahāsattvas to rouse their resolve to maintain [the Dharma] for future generations;

that those who hear it today do not fail to do so is entirely due to this. At Guangchen Town in Haiyan County, Xiu Prefecture, there was a monk named Chuanqian who once read this sutra and, looking up to revere the traces of the Buddha’s transformation, led the assembly of faithful to build a stupa based on the scripture, beginning from the Jiayou year of the cycle year Gui...
Mao Fa-shou began the construction during the Zhizhi and Pingji eras; unfortunately, he passed away. His disciple Zhiyuan was able to shoulder the master’s legacy and follow in his footsteps.

He applied himself with diligent effort, leaving no day of leisure for sixteen years until the second month of autumn in the first year of the Yuanfeng era (the Wuma year), when the labor was finally completed.
The expenses, amounting to no fewer than ten thousand strings of cash, were all provided from [his own resources].
Within the stupas for the fourfold assembly, there were seven tiers; in each tier was concealed a precious casket of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one fascicle per casket.

The lowest tier was inscribed with characters in gold and silver, and the topmost tier was fitted with a *cakra* (parasol). There were ninety-nine volumes of the scripture in total. Beneath the foundation, the śarīra of a reclining Buddha was enshrined.
As for the remaining scriptures, scrolls, and statues, their number cannot be fully enumerated. Within, a statue of Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni was sculpted.
The image of Kāśyapa sitting therein was adorned with various jewels, most exquisitely decorated; those who beheld it from afar or nearby marveled at its unprecedented nature.
Consequently, those who heard of or saw it turned away from heterodoxy and returned to the right path; those who paid homage had their transgressions extinguished and were graced with blessings.

Thus, upon encountering this object, their hearts were moved, and they immediately attained realization of the Way. They planted the seeds for the One Vehicle and established themselves within the realm of all Buddhas.

Such instances have occurred frequently. How profound! Master Chuan’s wisdom was initiated in his early years; through the perfection of his power, he employed conditioned means to establish great Buddhist services.

He brought forth the long-lost beauty of a thousand ages and served as a sublime guide for ten thousand kalpas. How can the benefits he brings to the world and the aid he provides to all beings be fully described?
Having followed this scripture and been able to investigate its beginning and end, I have ventured to take up my brush once more to compose this account.
The record states:
Regarding the inscription for the Amitābha image in the Immeasurable Courtyard,
although the teachings and contemplations concerning Amitābha recorded in the Tripitaka are by no means few, it has been several hundred years since the Buddha’s transformation reached the East.

In recent times, there have been few who truly understand this. Dharma Master Huiyuan of Jin resided at Donglin on Mount Lu; his spiritual faculties were uniquely transcendent, and he served as a pioneer for the world.
He planted lotuses by the imperial carriage-pool, constructed a hall, and made a vow to exclusively cultivate the Pure Land practice, naming it the White Lotus Society.
At that time, famous monks and great scholars arrived spontaneously without prior invitation—Huishizhi and Daosheng being the foremost among the Buddhist community.
The eminent and talented Liu Yimin and Lei Cizong, as well as the heroes among literary men, all humbled themselves to receive instruction and joined his society.
Therefore, when later generations speak of the Pure Land Societies (*jing-she*), they invariably begin with Donglin.

Subsequently, Shandao and Huigan extensively propagated the teaching in Chang’an, while Zhijue and Ciyun caused it to flourish greatly in the region south of the Zhejiang River; yet in its final stages, it became deranged.

Because the true path is obstructed by delusions, or because one is bound by names and forms, or because one sinks into a state of empty vacuity, there are those who disparage the practice of *nien-fo* as a coarse act, or neglect pure karma as a minor path.
Clinging to their own corners, they blind themselves and remain ignorant, hearing nothing at all; even if they hear, they do not believe;
even if they believe, they do not practice; and even if they practice, they lack diligence. Thus it is with regard to the teaching of the Pure Land school.
Or perhaps it has nearly been extinguished! Alas! As for the contemplation of the Bright Teaching (*Mingjiao guan*), who is its equal? Zhiyi (Zhe) was his peer;
at the end of his life, he recited the *Contemplation Sutra*, praised the Pure Land, and passed away. As for the realization of the Dharma-realm (*Fajie*), who is his equal? Du Shun was his peer;

he exhorted the fourfold assembly to contemplate Amitābha, and moved by the manifestation of the sublime signs, he departed toward the West. As for Chan practice and seeing one's nature, who is his equal? Gaofeng Yuanmiao and Zhijue were his peers; they all...
They formed a society for the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) and together ascended to the highest grade of rebirth.

Among those who studied the Confucian classics and possessed talent, who could compare to Liu Yuxi, Lei Zun, Liu Zongyuan, and Bai Juyi? Yet all of them took up their brushes to record their sincerity and expressed their vows to be born in that land.

Viewed from this perspective, who but one who possesses a firm, brilliant, and outstanding understanding, and who has mastered the principles of death, life, transformation, and change, could have done so?
Can one truly believe in this? In recent times, the great masters who possess impartiality and lack factionalism have generally used this method to instruct and guide their disciples.

Consequently, temples have been established and images fashioned everywhere; societies and assemblies have been formed such that, regardless of noble or humble status, young or old, all have returned their sincerity to the Pure Land.
Whether through visualization, recitation of the name, ritual chanting, or fasting and purification, there are even those who—

Those who beheld the radiant flowers, contemplated his marks and signs, witnessed the flow of his physical body into *śarīra*, or were moved by auspicious omens at the time of his passing are beyond counting;
the flourishing of such pure karma has had no equal since antiquity—how could one not feel fortunate to have been born at such a time?
Lin’an County is indeed a great district of Hangzhou, and Mount Jiuxian is its most excellent scenic site—limitless [is its merit].

The temple was also a sacred precinct. Previously, the practitioner had constructed an Avalokiteśvara Hall in the southeast corner of the temple grounds, and subsequently built an Amitābha Hall behind that hall.
His disciple Yongyuan then recruited one thousand men and women, raising a total of three hundred strings of cash to carve an eight-foot statue of Amitābha.
On the first day of the Lantern Festival in the eighth year of the Yuanyou era, they assembled.
When the multitude gazed upon and paid homage to Yuan, he recounted his realization by reciting verses and made a great vow; he then placed the image within its belly.
On that day, he provided offerings for five hundred arhats and held a feast to provide meals for the monastic community to consecrate it.

More than one year later, on the eighth day of the fourth month, the adornments were perfectly complete and the features were exquisitely beautiful, radiating with brilliant splendor. Consequently, the people of the region were able to take refuge and turn toward it.

For those who, even a hundred generations hence, are able to circulate this [teaching], there is no one who, upon seeing his honored countenance, calling his name, or sending forth thoughts of him with reverence, does not uproot the seeds of karma from the sea of suffering and cast the seeds of the lotus into the precious pond. As for those who paint on the ground or gather sand—each becomes a Buddha;
those who lower their heads or raise their hands all return to the One Vehicle. How much more so for those who exert themselves in practice and maintain sincere mindfulness!
If one were to weigh its benefits, how could they possibly be measured? Having heard that my intention lies in this Way, Yuan repeatedly requested a commemorative inscription;
I have therefore taken up the brush to write directly, thereby fulfilling his request.
Record of the Reconstruction of the Main Hall at Cide Monastery in Taizhou.
That which stores the *śarīra* (relics) of the Buddha from the land of Aparāntaka is called a *stūpa*; this is what is termed a "square mound" (*fangfen*).
That which enshrines the physical image of the Buddha is called a *caitya*; this is what is termed a "temple" (*miao*). However, that which is currently called a "hall" (*dian*) was originally...
The various names for "palace" (*gong*) have been used since the Qin and Han dynasties exclusively by those who are kings, for it is the dwelling place of the Most Honored One.

The Buddha is the Dharma-King who has emerged preeminent above all things; as the sovereign of transformation over the trichiliocosm and the guide of all living beings, his majesty may indeed be called ultimate.
Since the Buddha’s transformation first spread to the East, kings, dukes, and great ministers have honored his Way and revered his teaching, [regarding] both the mundane and the sacred.
Wherever such an image is located, it must be housed within a grand building distinguished by a magnificent name and designated as a "hall" (dian).

Thus, this tradition has been maintained through successive dynasties without decline. This monastery originally possessed a Buddha hall, but being crudely constructed and cramped from the start, it has gradually decayed over the years until it is now in a state of ruin.
Consequently, those who come to pay their respects are unable to manifest the utmost expression of reverence. — By the Venerable Subhūti.

Jian’s eldest son, Binbin, and his disciple Zhongyuan then conspired and exerted their combined efforts to solicit contributions from the public for the renovation of the great hall and the recasting of the sacred image.
Moved by their sincere devotion, the faithful responded in unison; thus, regardless of whether they were noble or humble, they all offered gold and silk.
The expenditure reached no less than two million coins, beginning in the Wuxu year of the Jiayou era.
Completed in the Dingwei year of the Zhiping era, its timber and construction are magnificent, its ridgepoles and rafters lofty and spacious, its golden hues radiant and its iconography peerless.
It is not merely a source of splendor for this single region, but shall serve as an object of veneration and aspiration for ten thousand generations.
I humbly reflect that the Tathāgata, with his Dharma-realm body, dwells in the Land of Quiescent Light—a realm pure, serene, vast, and profoundly still.
Words cannot fully express it, and the mind has no means to fathom it. As the Sūtra says: "The emptiness of nature is itself the Buddha; it cannot be grasped through thought. It also says:
"To be free from all marks is what is called the Buddhas. Thus one knows that the Buddha-body is not a physical form and that the Buddha-land has no fixed location.
Nevertheless, to enlighten those who are ignorant and to guide those who have lost their way, there is nothing better than manifesting this principle through concrete phenomena.
Because his marks could not move the mind, he appeared in the world; because he manifested a wondrous countenance, even after his parinirvāṇa, he displayed a majestic image.
Thus, Udayana first initiated [the tradition] in Western India, and Kāśyapa Mātanga brought it to Eastern Hua.
This became a supreme condition for generating merit and an easy path for transcending the world; therefore, people with distracted minds invoke his name.
All awakened to the Buddha-vehicle; with a raised hand or a lowered head, they all returned to the path of reality. Their merit is unfathomable and their benefit inexhaustible;

this is truly the essential gate of transformation and the fundamental basis for sustaining the Dharma. In the second month of winter in the second year of the Yuanyou era, I passed through this monastery on account of a commission to perform the ritual of boundary-binding (*sīmā-bandha*).
There, one Zhongyuan presented a formal document detailing the origins and circumstances of the matter, requesting a preface for it.
This inscription was composed because there was no other choice; I shall attempt to recount it once more.
The Record of the Dragon Spring Amitābha Pavilion in Yuezhou:

Gold, jade, and pearls are prized as the most precious things in the world, yet the deeds of moral virtue that transcend the world are revered by the Honored Ones and are rare, difficult to encounter, and extraordinary.

All these are called "jewels. However, the jewels that transcend the world are, in brief, fourfold: the Three Jewels of the One Essence, which are the innate, true nature inherent within the deluded thoughts of sentient beings;
the Three Jewels of the Essential Principle, which are the pure and undefiled fruits of the virtues of all Buddhas;

the Three Jewels of Transformational Manifestation, which appear at opportune times to benefit beings and enlighten the multitudes; and [the Three Jewels of] Bequeathed Legacy, which extend their bounty to future generations and flow forth without end.
The Three Jewels are sustained [as follows]: casting metal, molding clay, carving, and painting sustain the Buddha;

lacquered cases, gilded scrolls, paper, silk, bamboo, and cloth sustain the Dharma; and wearing ragged robes, altering one’s appearance, ascending the altar, and receiving the precepts sustain the Sangha.
Among the remaining Three Jewels, the Buddha is held most venerable; yet in sustaining the Three Jewels, the Sangha is ranked supreme—is this not because...?
Whether a thing flourishes, declines, or endures depends upon man. The Longquan Temple in Yu’ao, Yuezhou, began its construction during the Xiankang era of the Eastern Jin dynasty;
from then until the Dinghai year of the Daguang era, a total of eight hundred and fifty years have passed.

At the end of the Tang, during the Huichang persecution, the monasteries throughout the empire were systematically destroyed and abandoned; yet this stupa-temple alone remained solemnly intact, as the Xiantong era dawned.
As my Way was being restored, the Abbot of the temple, Dharma Master Faguang, exhorted local residents such as Zhan Wenju to transcribe and produce the Tripitaka.
In the second year of the Kaibao era of the Imperial Dynasty, the Venerable Huiwen first constructed a library pavilion to house the scriptures and receive visitors from all quarters.
In the second year of the Huangyou era, Zhidu and Yunxi joined forces in soliciting donations to separately establish a hall.

Furthermore, the Wheel Repository (Lun-zang) was subsequently abandoned and left unused within this repository pavilion. As many years passed, the buildings fell into ruin and decay, and the disciples were unable to repair them.
The presiding monks submitted a formal petition to the district magistrate, Mr. Zeng, who issued an official decree appointing Zhi-rong to succeed as the abbot.
Zhi-rong then exerted all his efforts to solicit contributions from the public, rebuilding and establishing the pavilion anew.
The temple consists of five bays in total, including those on the left, right, front, and back.

The abbot, Tan Yue, considering that the teachings and contemplations of the Pure Land school were flourishing at the time, provided his own funds to carve a majestic image of sixteen feet tall of Amitābha Buddha and installed it in the center.

He further arranged existing painted scrolls of the Thousand Buddhas and carved images of Avalokiteśvara (Da Bei) on either side, renovated the twin pagodas, expanded the hall, and increased the sacred relics.

He established a monastery and named it the "Precious Pavilion of Amitābha. From this point on, he was able to gather a community of monks to practice the Way and repay their gratitude, to uphold the monastic precepts, and to chant scriptures for the benefit of others.
Thus, the Three Jewels flourished and found peace, while the four classes of living beings gained a refuge upon which to rely.
This proves that the saying—"the Way has no rise or decline; its maintenance depends upon the person"—is not false. Great!
Record of the Revised Edition, Written on the Last Day of the Eighth Month.
Record of the Standing Images of the Three Sages at Jingyuan in Mingzhou.
Regarding the standing images of the Three Sages as seen in the *Contemplation Sūtra*: it is through the unconditioned great compassion of Śākyamuni Bhagavān [that they appear].

Out of profound compassion and endurance for those not yet delivered, he grandly inaugurated the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land and subtly revealed the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance (*nien-fo*), intending to cause sentient beings to take refuge in the pure realm.
Therefore, he established the sixteen wondrous contemplations (*śubha-vipaśyanā*) to focus the mind upon the sacred conditions.
Thus, the setting sun suspended like a drum points toward the direction [of the West], while the great waters freezing into ice represent the jeweled ground and groves.
As they gazed upon the towers and pavilions of the spring, there was nothing that was not adorned with a hundred jewels;
its radiance and brilliance were beyond compare in the world, such that its names could not be fully enumerated.

Just as they were about to extensively proclaim the observation of that Buddha’s body—its light, its marks, and its signs—and as the assembly was about to ascend toward goodness, suddenly within the great void of space, the Three Sages appeared for Vaidehī to behold.
To initiate this request, the Sūtra says: The Buddha addressed Vaidehī, "I shall now, for your sake, explain in detail the method for eliminating suffering and affliction.
As these words were spoken, Amitābha Buddha stood in mid-air, with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta standing in attendance at his left and right.
Vaidehī said to the Buddha, "By the power of the Buddha, I have now been able to see that [land]."
"How should future sentient beings contemplate the Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas so as to behold them?

The Buddha commanded that they first contemplate the flower throne, next contemplate the physical images, and finally contemplate the Buddha’s body along with his attendants on the left and right and the assemblies of the nine grades;
thus, the *Nien-fo San-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) is fully contained herein. Since the time of Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, monasteries throughout the world have bound themselves [to this practice].
The establishment of the Pure Society and the creation of the canopy for the Three Sages of Amitābha originated from this sutra; this is evident in these writings.

The monk Jieshen of Fuyuan Aranya on Mount Linggui in Cixi, Siming, entered the Path under the guidance of Vinaya Master Jingju and has constantly upheld this sutra while dedicating himself to the practice of the Pure Land for many years.
He believed that cultivating the Way for oneself alone was not as effective as encouraging others to do so.

The various people felt that a single moment of effort was not as good as preserving it for a long duration; thus, they organized a subscription among the faithful and went in person to Qiantang to commission artisans to carve standing statues of the Three Sages.
Traveling back and forth across a thousand li of mountains and rivers, they labored for several years before finally completing them at a cost of nearly one thousand strings of cash.
They were erected in the Sūtra Repository Hall of Kaiyuan Temple to the south of the city wall.

In his confession hall, the fourfold assembly gazed upon him with admiration, exclaiming that such a thing had never been seen before. One day, he took his boat across the river and arrived at the Zhizhen Aranya (Lanruo).
There, he opened his satchel to enter the summer retreat; incense was lit, and bowing his head, he requested a text to serve as a record.

Since I am one who takes this Way to heart, I am happy to write it down for him. Some may say: "The Sūtras state that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are the body of the Dharma-realm, entering into one..."

"If all sentient beings, within the thoughts of their minds, now carve wood to create images made of worldly materials and use these as substitutes for the Buddha—would this not be considered acceptable?
He replied, "The Buddha-body is without conceptual thought, yet it is not separate from form.

Because it is without [fixed] characteristics, there is not a single dharma, whether mundane or supramundane, that is the Buddha, even including the eighty-four thousand marks and the thirty-two major signs."
This is precisely because one does not use these marks to compare with other things; therefore it is said that being free from all marks is what constitutes the Buddhas.
Since they do not depart from marks, there is not a single phenomenon—whether mundane or supramundane—that is not the Buddha, let alone the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana).
Therefore it is said: "One should know that all dharmas are themselves the Buddha-dharma. If one can thus realize that marks are non-marks, [one attains this realization].

If that which is non-characteristic were not itself characteristic, then mountains, rivers, lands, grasses, trees, atoms, and the four modes of birth and six realms of existence—including all that flies, soars, crawls, and wriggles—would not be the substance of the Dharma-body of all Buddhas;

how much less could images cast in metal, molded from clay, carved in wood, or painted on silk, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, fail to be the Buddha? Those who possess wisdom should contemplate these images as being made of timber, bamboo, cloth, and thread.
Adhesives, lacquer, gold, and pigments are merely provisionally manifested through the combination of various conditions.

If one seeks [the Buddha] within these conditions, they are all worldly things, each possessing its own name and substance; which among them could be the Buddha? However, since conditions have no fixed characteristics and things have no fixed names, once something is designated as "Buddha," then all conditions are none other than the essence of the Buddha.
How could one abandon these and seek the Buddha elsewhere? Therefore, the Avataṃsaka...
Yan said: "Form and appearance are not the Buddha; sound and voice are likewise so. Yet, one does not perceive the Buddha apart from form and sound—such is the power of his spiritual penetrations.
If one contemplates the image without dwelling upon its marks, nor yet being separated from those marks, then principle and phenomenon are as one, and the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual.
Although one faces the image, this is truly seeing the Buddha. As the Sūtra says: "If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one constructs and establishes images..."
To uphold and offer these to such persons ensures that they will surely attain the Pure Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha in future lives.

Thus we know that during the Dharma-ending Age, maintaining the physical representations of the Buddha is supreme; there are none among those of superior, middling, or inferior faculties who do not receive benefit.

Therefore, King Udayana first carved [an image] from red sandalwood in the Western Land of the *Sakyas*, and Kāśyapa Mātanga first brought the white cotton cloth and the painted image to the Eastern Continent of *Jambudvīpa* to transmit the model.

Since these auspicious responses have been so extensive, sentient beings who behold these signs know where to turn for refuge, and having received the transformative influence of the Buddha’s teaching, they remain long within its wind.

Those with conscious minds who penetrate the fundamental source directly ascend to the Supreme Vehicle; even those who merely raise a hand or lower their head ultimately plant the seeds of conditions.
To speak of the vastness of their salvation, how could it be fully described? Whenever one arrives at a site of the Way, one ought to exercise the utmost vigilance and reverence.
Supplement to the Zhīyuán jí (Anthology from the Garden of Mushrooms)
